items.title: L8: Editing and managing a long document
items.source: GOV.UK content design guidance; Government Digital Service: writing for GOV.UK; National Archives guidance on version control
items.body:
A long report or guidance document needs a structure that readers can navigate. Begin with a summary of one page or less that gives the main findings, the conclusion and any recommendation, written last but placed first. Many readers will read only the summary and the headings, so each heading should say what the section tells them. 'Why the backlog grew in 2024' tells a reader more than 'Analysis'.

Use signposting. Tell the reader at the start what the document covers and how it is organised, and use clear transitions between sections. Keep a consistent order within similar sections, for example 'what we found, what it means, what we will do'. Use the same term for the same thing throughout: if a paper switches between 'customers', 'claimants' and 'clients', readers wonder if they are different groups.

Check consistency across the document. Numbers in the summary must match the numbers in the body. Cross-references such as 'see section 4' must point to the right place, and a table's title must match its content. When you cut text, look for references that now point nowhere.

Control versions. Name drafts clearly, for example 'Backlog report v0.3 draft', and save changes under a new number so that colleagues do not work on the wrong copy. Use tracked changes when several people edit, and agree who holds the master copy. Do not circulate two live versions. Remove tracked changes, comments and hidden text before you publish, as readers can often view them, and check the document properties for names and other metadata.

Ask a colleague who has not seen the work to read it cold. If they cannot say what you want from them after the first page, redraft the opening. Finally, read the final version in full, because late edits are the most common source of errors.

questions.prompt: Where should the summary of a long report be placed, and when should it be written?

options.text: At the front, and written last once the findings are settled
In the middle, written alongside the findings
At the end, written first so that it can guide the research and the structure
In an annex, written by a second author

questions.hint: A summary has to reflect the final content but must be the first thing the reader sees.

questions.prompt: Which heading is most useful to a reader scanning a report?

options.text: Why the backlog grew during 2024
Further considerations
Section 3
Analysis

questions.hint: A heading that states the content tells scanning readers what the section says.

questions.prompt: A report calls the same group 'customers' in one section, 'claimants' in another and 'clients' elsewhere. What is the problem?

options.text: The document will be longer than it needs to be
The report breaks a rule about using more than one noun
Readers may think these are different groups
The headings will no longer match the contents

questions.hint: Consistent terms avoid confusing the reader about who is being discussed.

questions.prompt: You delete section 4 from a draft. What should you check?

options.text: That no cross-reference elsewhere still points to section 4
That the remaining sections are renumbered in alphabetical order of their headings
That the page count is a round number
That the summary is longer than before

questions.hint: Deleted material often leaves behind references that no longer make sense.

questions.prompt: The summary says 1,240 cases but a table in section 2 shows 1,420. What should you do?

options.text: Remove the table so the figures cannot be compared
Find which figure is correct against the source and correct whichever is wrong
Change the table to match the summary without checking, since the summary was written by a senior colleague
Leave both, because the summary is rounded

questions.hint: Inconsistent figures undermine trust, so check the source before correcting.

questions.prompt: Which file name gives the clearest version information?

options.text: Backlog report latest
Backlog report v0.3 draft
Backlog report new copy
Backlog report final

questions.hint: A version number lets people see which copy is current and what came before.

questions.prompt: Before publishing a document that several colleagues edited, what must you do with tracked changes and comments?

options.text: Leave them in so readers can see how the document developed and who suggested each change
Hide them by changing the font colour to white
Convert the file to a lower resolution
Resolve them and remove them, and check the document properties for hidden data

questions.hint: Tracked changes and metadata can reveal drafts, names and comments.

questions.prompt: Two colleagues have each saved their own edited copies of the same paper. What is the best way to avoid this problem next time?

options.text: Keep both copies and merge them by hand when the paper is finished
Agree one master copy and who edits it, and number new versions
Ask everyone to email their copy to the whole team
Let each author decide how to name their file

questions.hint: One controlled master avoids conflicting changes and lost edits.

questions.prompt: A colleague who has not seen the paper reads page one and cannot say what you want from them. What does this suggest?

options.text: The paper should be turned into a presentation
The paper needs more background at the start
The opening needs redrafting to state the purpose and ask
The colleague needs training in reading reports

questions.hint: A cold read is a test of whether the opening works for new readers.

questions.prompt: Why should you read the whole document through after the final edit?

options.text: Because the template requires it
Because the summary has to be re-timed
Because tracked changes cannot be removed otherwise
Late changes are a common source of new errors

questions.hint: A last edit can break figures, references or formatting.

items.title: L8: Explaining a complex decision to the public
items.source: GOV.UK style guide; Plain English Campaign guidance; Parliamentary and Health Service Ombudsman Principles of Good Administration
items.body:
When a decision rests on a calculation or a rule, the customer needs to see how you got there. Start with the decision and the amount. Then show the steps in order, using a short table or numbered list. Give each step in words as well as figures. Explain any term the customer will not know. Avoid words such as 'disregard' or 'apportion' without an explanation, or use a plainer alternative such as 'not counted' and 'shared out'.

Suppose a benefit is reduced because of other income. Rather than writing 'Your award has been recalculated in line with regulation 7', say: 'We have reduced your payment from £480 to £320 a month. This is because you started to receive £400 a month from a pension, and we count 40% of this as income.' Then show the sum in a list: Pension £400, 40% counted £160, new payment £480 minus £160, which is £320. The aim is that the reader can check it, and challenge it if they think it is wrong.

Use a consistent layout. Put the key action near the top, and use headings that say what comes next. Short paragraphs and lists help, but do not break up sentences that need to stay together.

If a customer is asked to repay money after an overpayment, explain why it happened, how much was overpaid, the period it covers and what choices they have, such as repaying in instalments. Do not blame the customer if the department made the error, and say clearly whether the debt must be repaid. Give the details of how to dispute it.

Where the audience includes people who do not read English well, offer translation and signpost interpreter services. The Ombudsman's principles ask that public bodies are customer focused, open and accountable, act fairly and proportionately, and put things right when they go wrong.

Test letters on people who are not experts in the subject.

questions.prompt: What should a letter that reduces a payment put first?

options.text: A request for any new information
A list of the other benefits the customer may claim
The decision and the new amount
An explanation of the legal framework

questions.hint: Readers want the outcome immediately, before the explanation.

questions.prompt: Which sentence best explains a reduction in payment?

options.text: We have reduced your payment from £480 to £320 a month because your pension counts as income.
Your award has been recalculated in line with regulation 7.
An adjustment has been made to your entitlement in accordance with the rules.
Your payment has changed following a review of your circumstances.

questions.hint: The plainest version gives the old and new amounts and the reason in everyday words.

questions.prompt: Why show the calculation in a short list or table?

options.text: So that the letter looks longer and more official, which makes customers trust the decision
So that no explanation in words is needed
So that the legal wording can be removed
So that the reader can check it and challenge it if they think it is wrong

questions.hint: A visible calculation helps people understand and, if necessary, dispute the result.

questions.prompt: A pension of £400 a month counts as income at 40%, and the claim is £480. Which payment is correct?

options.text: £320, because 40% of £400 is £160 and 480 minus 160 is 320
£440, because 40% of £400 is £40
£400, because the pension is taken off the claim in full
£80, because 480 minus 400 is 80

questions.hint: The counted income is 0.4 x 400 = £160, which is deducted from £480.

questions.prompt: Which term would most need a plain explanation in a letter to the public?

options.text: Pay
Reduce
Apportion
Month

questions.hint: Technical words like 'apportion' should be explained or replaced by 'share out'.

questions.prompt: A department made an error that led to an overpayment. How should the letter treat the customer?

options.text: Say the customer should have noticed the mistake and told the department about it much sooner
Leave out the cause to avoid confusion
Demand immediate repayment of the full amount
Explain the error, avoid blaming the customer, and set out the options for repayment

questions.hint: Customer-focused administration is open about what went wrong and treats people fairly.

questions.prompt: What should an overpayment letter say about the debt?

options.text: The names of the staff who made the mistake and the action taken against them afterwards
How much, what period it covers and whether it must be repaid, with how to dispute it
Only that the debt is being reviewed
Only the total owed and the date it is due

questions.hint: People need the facts of the debt and their rights to query it.

questions.prompt: Which of the Ombudsman's Principles of Good Administration asks a body to correct a mistake and make amends?

options.text: Being open and accountable
Seeking continuous improvement
Getting it right
Putting things right

questions.hint: This principle covers acknowledging mistakes, apologising and providing a fair remedy.

questions.prompt: What is a good way to test a complex letter before you send it?

options.text: Read it aloud to the policy team who wrote the rule
Ask the legal team to approve the wording only
Run it through a grammar checker alone
Ask someone who is not an expert in the subject to read it

questions.hint: A non-expert is likely to find the confusing parts that experts miss.

questions.prompt: A customer does not read English well. Which is the most helpful addition to the letter?

options.text: The statutory text in an annex
A note on how to get a translation or an interpreter
A longer paragraph of explanation in English
A request that they bring a friend to translate

questions.hint: Offering translation or interpreting support removes a barrier to understanding.

items.title: L8: Making documents accessible
items.source: Public Sector Bodies (Websites and Mobile Applications) (No. 2) Accessibility Regulations 2018; GOV.UK guidance on making documents accessible; Equality Act 2010
items.body:
Accessibility means that people with disabilities can use what you produce, including people who use screen readers, have low vision, have dyslexia or have difficulty with fine motor control. Under the Equality Act 2010, public bodies must make reasonable adjustments, and the Public Sector Bodies (Websites and Mobile Applications) (No. 2) Accessibility Regulations 2018 require public sector websites and apps to meet the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) at level AA and to publish an accessibility statement. Documents published on a website are covered as well.

For documents, use the built-in styles for headings rather than making text bigger or bold. Screen readers use real headings to navigate. Give the document a title and keep the heading order logical, without skipping levels. Use real lists, not typed dashes, and do not leave blank lines to create space.

Add alternative text to images that carry meaning, describing what the image shows and why it matters. Decorative images can be marked as decorative. Do not put important information in an image of text, because a screen reader cannot read it.

Do not rely on colour alone. If a chart uses red and green to show good and bad, add labels or patterns, because some readers cannot tell them apart. Check that text has enough contrast against its background, since pale grey on white is hard to read.

Use simple tables with clear header rows. Avoid merged cells, which confuse screen readers. Use link text that describes the destination, and avoid long strings of capitals. Use sans serif fonts at a sensible size, left-aligned text, and avoid justified text because uneven spacing can cause problems for some readers.

GOV.UK prefers HTML pages to PDFs because they adapt to different devices and assistive technologies. If a PDF is needed, make it from an accessible source with tags so that the structure is preserved. Always offer another format on request.

questions.prompt: What is the correct way to create a heading in a Word document that will be read by a screen reader?

options.text: Apply a built-in heading style
Make the text larger and bold
Underline the text and add a colon
Type it in capitals and add a blank line

questions.hint: Screen readers navigate by real heading styles, not by appearance.

questions.prompt: Which statement about alternative text is correct?

options.text: It should repeat the file name of the image so that the reader can find the original file
It is needed only for photographs of people
It should describe what an image shows and why it matters when the image carries meaning
It is never needed if there is a caption

questions.hint: Alt text tells screen reader users what the image conveys.

questions.prompt: A chart uses red and green bars for good and poor performance. What should be added?

options.text: Labels or patterns so the difference is clear without colour
A darker shade of red and green
A legend in a smaller font
A third colour for the average

questions.hint: Some people cannot distinguish red and green, so colour should not be the only cue.

questions.prompt: Why should you avoid using blank lines to space out content?

options.text: Blank lines make files larger than the size permitted for publication on a government website
They are not allowed by the Equality Act 2010
They break the line spacing rules for GOV.UK
Screen readers announce empty lines and the structure becomes harder to follow

questions.hint: Use spacing settings and proper structure rather than empty paragraphs.

questions.prompt: Which table design is best for accessibility?

options.text: A table that has been pasted as a picture
A table with coloured shading but no header row
A table with merged cells for the main headings
A simple table with a clear header row and no merged cells

questions.hint: Simple structure lets assistive technology read cells in order.

questions.prompt: Which level of WCAG must public sector websites meet under the 2018 Regulations?

options.text: A
AAA
AA
B

questions.hint: The regulations require WCAG at level AA and an accessibility statement.

questions.prompt: Why does GOV.UK usually prefer HTML pages to PDFs?

options.text: HTML pages need no accessibility testing
PDFs cannot contain text
They adapt to different devices and assistive technologies
They are always smaller files

questions.hint: HTML responds to the user's settings and device, which PDFs do not do easily.

questions.prompt: A document has an important notice inside a screenshot of text. What is the problem?

options.text: The image file is too large to publish
The notice will not print in colour
The image cannot be given a caption
A screen reader cannot read the text in an image

questions.hint: Information should be in real text, not locked in images.

questions.prompt: Which text alignment is best for readability for most users?

options.text: Right-aligned
Centred
Justified
Left-aligned

questions.hint: Justified text can create uneven gaps that make reading harder, and left alignment gives a consistent start.

questions.prompt: A reader asks for a document in Easy Read. What does the Equality Act 2010 expect the department to do?

options.text: Provide it only after the next review of the guidance
Consider it as a reasonable adjustment and provide it unless it is not reasonable
Ask the reader for a medical certificate first
Refuse because the standard version is already published and the department has met its duty

questions.hint: Public bodies have a duty to make reasonable adjustments for disabled people.

items.title: L8: Handling a complaint when the department was at fault
items.source: Parliamentary and Health Service Ombudsman: Principles of Good Administration, Principles of Remedy; Civil Service Code
items.body:
When a complaint shows that the department got something wrong, the response needs to do four things: acknowledge the error, apologise, put things right, and explain what will change. An apology should be sincere and specific. 'We are sorry that we sent your payment to the wrong account, and that you went without it for three weeks' is better than 'we apologise for any inconvenience'. An apology is not an admission of legal liability in the sense of inviting a claim, and it should not be withheld for that reason.

The Ombudsman's Principles of Remedy say that, where possible, a public body should return the person to the position they would have been in if the poor service had not occurred. If that is not possible, it should consider compensation or another suitable remedy. A remedy might include paying money owed, correcting records, and reimbursing costs that the person incurred because of the error, such as bank charges. Where there has been distress or inconvenience, a modest payment may be appropriate. A remedy should be proportionate to the impact.

Find the cause. A one-off slip by an individual is different from a flaw in a process. If many customers could be affected by the same problem, tell the line manager so it can be fixed. Under the Civil Service Code, officials should be honest and should not deceive or mislead, so do not blame the customer for errors the department made and do not hide mistakes.

Keep the customer informed about timescales. Explain how to take the complaint further if they are unhappy with the response, including the right to ask an MP to refer it to the Ombudsman.

Record what went wrong and what was done in the complaints log, so that patterns can be analysed.

questions.prompt: Which apology is best in a complaint response?

options.text: We apologise for any inconvenience this may have caused.
We regret that you feel your payment was not handled well.
We are sorry if you were upset by the delay in your payment.
We are sorry that we sent your payment to the wrong account and that you went without it for three weeks.

questions.hint: A specific apology that names what went wrong shows the department has understood the problem.

questions.prompt: What do the Ombudsman's Principles of Remedy aim to do where possible?

options.text: Return the person to the position they would have been in if the problem had not happened
Punish the member of staff responsible
Offer the same fixed sum in every complaint so that remedies are consistent whatever the harm
Close the complaint as quickly as possible

questions.hint: The primary aim of a remedy is to put things back as they should have been.

questions.prompt: A bank charged a customer £25 because the department's payment arrived late. How should the response deal with this?

options.text: Explain that the department is not liable for bank charges that a third party applies
Refuse because the sum is too small to count
Reimburse the bank charge as a cost caused by the department's error
Tell the customer to claim it back from the bank

questions.hint: Costs that arise directly from the error are part of putting things right.

questions.prompt: Why should the department explain what will change after an error?

options.text: It allows the department to close the complaint file
It is a legal requirement in every case
It removes the customer's right to complain further
It shows that the department has learned from the problem and reduces the chance of it happening again

questions.hint: Learning from complaints is a key part of good administration.

questions.prompt: A complaint shows a fault in a template letter used for hundreds of customers. What should the complaint handler do?

options.text: Fix the single customer's letter only
Wait for more customers to complain
Report the fault to the manager so it can be fixed and others put right
Tell the customer the template is correct and that other customers have not complained

questions.hint: A systemic flaw affects many people and needs wider action.

questions.prompt: Why might a department hesitate to apologise, and why is that hesitation wrong?

options.text: It might fear admitting liability, but a sincere apology is not an admission that invites a claim
Apologies are only for the Ombudsman to give
Apologies create a duty to pay compensation
Apologies are not allowed in written responses because they can be used as evidence in a court case

questions.hint: An apology is good practice and does not prevent the department from defending a legal claim.

questions.prompt: A customer was told wrongly that they owed money, and the department made the mistake. Which wording follows the Civil Service Code's honesty value?

options.text: A discrepancy arose in the recording of your account.
It appears that some confusion arose about the debt.
You may have misunderstood our earlier letter.
The error was ours: we told you wrongly that you owed money, and you do not.

questions.hint: Honesty means owning up to errors and not shifting blame.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of the complaints log?

options.text: To prove that the customer was wrong
To store the customer's personal details for marketing and for later use by other teams
To record what went wrong and what was done so patterns can be analysed
To rank staff by number of complaints

questions.hint: Analysing trends helps to fix root causes.

questions.prompt: After a final response, what must the department tell a dissatisfied customer?

options.text: How to take the complaint further, including referral to the Ombudsman through an MP
Only the name of the manager who signed the letter
That the matter is now closed and cannot be reviewed by anyone else once the final response is sent
That the Ombudsman will need to be paid a fee

questions.hint: Customers should be told how to escalate if they are not satisfied.

questions.prompt: When might a modest payment for distress or inconvenience be appropriate?

options.text: When the error caused real stress or hassle in addition to financial loss
Whenever a customer complains, whatever the facts, so that complaints are settled quickly
Only when the customer has hired a solicitor
Never, because compensation is for courts only

questions.hint: Remedies should be proportionate to the impact of the poor service.

items.title: L8: Spreadsheets: XLOOKUP in depth
items.body:
XLOOKUP has the form =XLOOKUP(lookup_value, lookup_array, return_array, [if_not_found], [match_mode], [search_mode]). Unlike VLOOKUP, it can look to the left, returns exactly the array you choose, and defaults to an exact match.

The match_mode argument has four settings. 0 is an exact match, the default. -1 gives an exact match or, failing that, the next smaller item. 1 gives an exact match or the next larger item. 2 allows wildcard characters, so "Lee*" matches any text beginning Lee. The data does not need to be sorted for any of these.

The search_mode argument sets the direction. 1 searches from first to last, the default. -1 searches from last to first, so it returns the last match when there are duplicates. 2 and -2 are for binary search on sorted data and are rarely needed.

Consider a table with references in A2:A5 (R1, R2, R3, R4) and officers in B2:B5 (Amy, Raj, Amy, Lee). =XLOOKUP("Amy",B2:B5,A2:A5) returns R1, the first match. Adding search_mode -1, =XLOOKUP("Amy",B2:B5,A2:A5,"None",0,-1), returns R3, the last. =XLOOKUP("Lee*",B2:B5,A2:A5,,2) returns R4.

Now consider a thresholds table with limits 100, 250, 500 and 1000 in D2:D5 and rates 1%, 2%, 3% and 5% in E2:E5. =XLOOKUP(300,D2:D5,E2:E5,,-1) returns 2%, as 250 is the next smaller limit. With match_mode 1 it returns 3%, as 500 is the next larger. =XLOOKUP(50,D2:D5,E2:E5,"Below range",-1) returns the text Below range, since no smaller threshold exists.

The return array can have several columns, which makes XLOOKUP spill a whole row of results into neighbouring cells. Make sure those cells are empty, or the formula returns #SPILL!.

XLOOKUP is available in current versions of Excel, but not in very old ones, so check that colleagues can open the file.

questions.prompt: With references R1 to R4 in A2:A5 and officers Amy, Raj, Amy, Lee in B2:B5, what does =XLOOKUP("Amy",B2:B5,A2:A5) return?

options.text: R3
R1
Raj
#N/A

questions.hint: With the default search mode, the first match is returned.

questions.prompt: How do you get XLOOKUP to return the last match for Amy?

options.text: Set match_mode to -1
Sort the officers in reverse order
Add an asterisk to the lookup value
Set the search_mode argument to -1

questions.hint: A search mode of -1 searches from the last item back to the first.

questions.prompt: What does =XLOOKUP("Amy",B2:B5,A2:A5,"None",0,-1) return?

options.text: R3
#VALUE!
None
R1

questions.hint: It searches from last to first, so the later Amy row is found first.

questions.prompt: Which setting lets XLOOKUP use wildcards such as Lee*?

options.text: match_mode 0
match_mode 2
search_mode 2
if_not_found set to an asterisk

questions.hint: Wildcard matching is switched on by match_mode 2.

questions.prompt: Thresholds 100, 250, 500, 1000 have rates 1%, 2%, 3%, 5%. What does =XLOOKUP(300,D2:D5,E2:E5,,-1) return?

options.text: #N/A

questions.hint: match_mode -1 returns the next smaller limit, which is 250.

questions.prompt: What does the same lookup return if match_mode is changed to 1?

options.text: #N/A

questions.hint: match_mode 1 returns the next larger item, which is 500.

questions.prompt: What does =XLOOKUP(50,D2:D5,E2:E5,"Below range",-1) return?

options.text: Below range
#N/A

questions.hint: No threshold is smaller than 50, so the if_not_found text is shown.

questions.prompt: Which feature makes XLOOKUP better than VLOOKUP when the result column is left of the key column?

options.text: It never returns errors
It can return from any array, to the left or right
It always gives approximate matches
It sorts the table first

questions.hint: XLOOKUP's separate lookup and return arrays remove VLOOKUP's left-to-right limit.

questions.prompt: An XLOOKUP that returns several columns shows #SPILL!. What is the usual cause?

options.text: The cells it would fill already contain data
The formula was copied from another sheet
The lookup value is text
The workbook is protected

questions.hint: A spilling formula needs empty space for its full result.

questions.prompt: What is a risk of using XLOOKUP in a shared workbook?

options.text: Colleagues using very old versions of Excel may not be able to calculate it
It deletes the source table and keeps only the first match it finds in the data
It cannot return text
It converts numbers to text

questions.hint: Older software does not recognise newer functions, resulting in errors.

items.title: L8: Spreadsheets: combining functions with SUMPRODUCT and IFERROR
items.source: Microsoft Support: SUMPRODUCT, IFERROR and INDEX with MATCH
items.body:
SUMPRODUCT multiplies matching items in ranges and adds up the products. With one range per argument, =SUMPRODUCT(B2:B7,C2:C7) multiplies each pair and then totals them. It is helpful for weighted totals. You can also add conditions: =SUMPRODUCT((A2:A7="North")*(B2:B7)) adds the values in B only where column A says North, because the test returns 1 or 0 for each row. Each range must be the same size.

Use this data. Column A has regions: North, South, North, East, South, North. Column B has cases: 12, 8, 15, 6, 11, 9. Column C has the proportion upheld: 0.5, 0.4, 0.6, 0.3, 0.45, 0.55.

=SUMPRODUCT(B2:B7,C2:C7) gives the total number of cases upheld: 6 + 3.2 + 9 + 1.8 + 4.95 + 4.95, which is 29.9. =SUMPRODUCT((A2:A7="North")*B2:B7*C2:C7) gives the upheld cases in the North, 19.95. The North had 36 cases (12, 15 and 9), so the weighted upheld rate for the North is 19.95 divided by 36, which is 0.554, or 55.4 per cent. The simple average of the three North rates (0.5, 0.6, 0.55) is 0.55, a slightly different answer, because the larger case counts carry more weight in the weighted result.

Combine functions carefully. =IFERROR(INDEX(C2:C7,MATCH("West",A2:A7,0)),"No West cases") returns a message instead of #N/A when West is not in the list. The inner functions are evaluated first, then the outer ones. When a formula is long, build it in stages in helper cells and test each stage, then combine.

Brackets matter. Count opening and closing brackets, and use the colour matching in the formula bar. A formula with a missing bracket will not be accepted, and one with misplaced brackets may give an answer that looks plausible but is wrong.

Do not use SUMPRODUCT with text in the number ranges: text is treated as zero.

questions.prompt: What does =SUMPRODUCT(B2:B7,C2:C7) calculate for the cases and proportions upheld?

options.text: The average proportion upheld, 0.5
The total number of cases, 61
The number of rows, 6
The total number of cases upheld, 29.9

questions.hint: Each case count is multiplied by its proportion and the products are added.

questions.prompt: What does =SUMPRODUCT((A2:A7="North")*B2:B7) return?
questions.hint: It adds the cases (12, 15 and 9) only for North rows.

questions.prompt: What is the weighted upheld rate for the North, as a percentage to one decimal place?
questions.hint: 19.95 upheld cases divided by 36 cases is about 0.554.

questions.prompt: Why does the weighted North rate differ from the simple average of 0.5, 0.6 and 0.55?

options.text: The simple average ignores the highest value
Weighted rates always come out lower
Excel rounds the weighted figure differently
Larger groups carry more weight in the weighted calculation

questions.hint: Weighting reflects the number of cases behind each rate.

questions.prompt: Which formula returns a message if West does not appear in A2:A7?

options.text: =IF(MATCH("West",A2:A7,0),"No West cases")
=INDEX(C2:C7,MATCH("West",A2:A7,0),"No West cases")
=MATCH("West",A2:A7,0)&"No West cases"
=IFERROR(INDEX(C2:C7,MATCH("West",A2:A7,0)),"No West cases")

questions.hint: IFERROR catches the #N/A from MATCH and shows the text instead.

questions.prompt: In a nested formula, which part does Excel evaluate first?

options.text: The outermost function
The function furthest to the left
The innermost function
The function with the longest name

questions.hint: Excel works from the inside out, so inner results feed outer functions.

questions.prompt: A SUMPRODUCT returns #VALUE!. What is a likely cause?

options.text: The workbook has no named ranges
The formula has no IF function
The ranges contain numbers
The ranges are different sizes

questions.hint: All arrays in a SUMPRODUCT must have the same dimensions.

questions.prompt: What is a sensible approach when building a long formula?

options.text: Hide the sheet so that errors are not noticed
Build and test it in stages using helper cells
Copy a similar formula and change numbers randomly
Write it in one go and trust the result

questions.hint: Staged testing makes errors easier to find.

items.title: L8: Spreadsheets: working days and service levels
items.source: Microsoft Support: WORKDAY, NETWORKDAYS functions; GOV.UK bank holidays
items.body:
Service levels often count working days from the day a case is received. Excel's WORKDAY function gives the due date: =WORKDAY(start_date, days, [holidays]). It skips Saturdays and Sundays, and any dates listed in the holidays range. NETWORKDAYS(start, end, [holidays]) counts the working days between two dates, including both the start and the end date if they are working days.

Suppose a case is received on Thursday 10 April 2025 and the target is 10 working days. With no holidays listed, =WORKDAY(A2,10) returns Thursday 24 April 2025. The 2025 Good Friday (18 April) and Easter Monday (21 April) were bank holidays in England and Wales. If both are in the holiday list, the same formula returns Monday 28 April 2025.

Counting the other way, NETWORKDAYS from 10 April to 30 April 2025 returns 15 with no holidays, and 13 with the two bank holidays listed. Remember that NETWORKDAYS includes the first day, so a case received and answered on the same working day counts as 1.

Keep the holiday dates in one named range on a separate sheet, so every formula uses the same list and the list can be updated in one place. Bank holidays differ between England and Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland, so use the right list for the office. GOV.UK publishes the official dates.

A breach flag can be built with =IF(closed_date>due_date,"Breach","Within target"). Use closed dates that are real dates, not text, and handle open cases with a test, since a blank closed date counts as zero. For open cases, compare TODAY() with the due date instead.

If a team works different days, use NETWORKDAYS.INTL and WORKDAY.INTL, which let you choose which days are weekends.

questions.prompt: A case is received on Thursday 10 April 2025 with a 10-working-day target and no holidays listed. What does =WORKDAY(A2,10) return?

options.text: Thursday 24 April 2025
Monday 28 April 2025
Sunday 20 April 2025
Friday 25 April 2025

questions.hint: Ten weekdays after Thursday 10 April is two weeks later.

questions.prompt: With Good Friday (18 April) and Easter Monday (21 April) in the holiday list, what is the due date?

options.text: Tuesday 29 April 2025

questions.hint: The two holidays push the due date back by two working days.

questions.prompt: With the same holidays listed, what does NETWORKDAYS from 10 April to 30 April 2025 return?
questions.hint: There are 15 weekdays and 2 of them are holidays.

questions.prompt: Why does NETWORKDAYS return 1 when the start and end date are the same working day?

options.text: It ignores the end date

questions.hint: Both ends are included in the count.

questions.hint: Using the wrong list would give wrong due dates in some offices.

items.title: L8: Spreadsheets: reading and building pivot tables
items.source: Microsoft Support: PivotTable calculations, grouping and slicers
items.body:
A pivot table can do more than sum. In Value Field Settings you can show values as a percentage of the grand total, row total or column total. You can also group dates by month or quarter, group numbers into ranges, and add slicers, which are buttons for filtering. A calculated field lets you add a formula, such as dividing one field by another, though it works on the sums of fields, which can give a misleading ratio. Check any calculated field against a manual calculation.

Consider this complaints data: Housing Q1 30, Housing Q2 50, Benefits Q1 60, Benefits Q2 40, Housing Q1 20, Passports Q2 25, Passports Q1 15, Benefits Q2 10. A pivot table with Service in rows and the sum of Complaints in values gives Housing 100, Benefits 110, Passports 40 and a grand total of 250. Shown as a percentage of the grand total, these are 40%, 44% and 16%. With Quarter in columns, the totals for Q1 and Q2 are each 125. For Benefits only, Q1 is 60 and Q2 is 50.

Common causes of wrong pivots are inconsistent labels in the source data, such as 'Housing' and 'housing ' with a trailing space, which can create two separate rows; numbers stored as text that are counted not summed; blank cells in the key fields; and duplicate records that inflate totals. Always clean the source before building the pivot table.

A pivot table is not live. After changing the source you must refresh it. Be wary of sharing a pivot table file, because the pivot cache can hold the full source data even when you show only a summary. Anyone with the file may be able to see detail you intended to hide, including personal data.

Label the pivot table clearly, remove the grand total if it misleads, and say what the numbers count: complaints, cases or people.

questions.prompt: In the complaints data, what percentage of all complaints relates to Benefits?
questions.hint: Benefits has 110 of the 250 complaints.

questions.hint: The Benefits rows in Q2 are 40 and 10.

questions.hint: A numeric field stored as text defaults to Count.

questions.prompt: Why might a pivot table total be too high?

The slicers are set to all

questions.hint: Duplicates inflate totals, so clean data first.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of slicers in a pivot table?

options.text: They convert the pivot table to a chart

questions.hint: Slicers make filtering visible and interactive.

options.text: It can only add numbers

questions.hint: The ratio is computed from the sums, which may differ from the average of row ratios.

questions.prompt: You send a colleague an Excel file with a pivot table showing only a summary. What privacy risk remains?

questions.hint: Hidden source data can usually be recovered, so share a values-only summary if detail must stay private.

options.text: Asks you to retype the data

questions.hint: Refresh is a manual action by default.

items.title: L8: Spreadsheets: keeping data accurate with validation and tables
items.source: Microsoft Support: data validation, conditional formatting, Excel tables, protect a worksheet; Government Analysis Function guidance on spreadsheets
items.body:
Good spreadsheets prevent errors as well as detect them. Data validation restricts what can be entered in a cell. You can limit entries to a list (a drop-down), a whole number between two values, or a date range, and add an input message and an error alert. A drop-down for 'Region' prevents the variants 'North West', 'N West' and 'NW' that damage counts and pivot tables. Validation only applies to what is typed after it is set up, and pasted values can bypass it.

Conditional formatting changes the appearance of cells according to rules. It can highlight overdue dates, duplicate values or the top ten per cent. It is a visual aid; it does not change values.

Convert a range to an Excel table (Ctrl+T) and it gains a name, filters, automatic expansion when you add rows, and structured references such as =SUM(Cases[Closed]). Formulas that refer to the table pick up new rows automatically, so totals do not miss them.

Named ranges give a cell or range a meaningful name, like VAT_rate, so formulas are easier to read. Freeze panes keeps headings visible when you scroll. Remove Duplicates deletes repeated rows, but check first that what you consider a duplicate is in fact a duplicate, because it cannot always be undone once saved.

Text to columns splits one column into several, for example splitting 'Smith, Jane' at the comma. TRIM removes stray spaces. If numbers are stored as text, they show a green triangle and left-align; convert them with VALUE or by multiplying by 1.

Protect a sheet to stop accidental changes to formulas: unlock the input cells, then turn on protection. A protection password is not strong security and should not be used to hide sensitive data.

Document the assumptions and sources on a separate sheet, and keep inputs, calculations and outputs apart.

options.text: Freeze panes

questions.hint: Use proper access controls and remove sensitive data instead.

items.title: L8: Sharing data between organisations: gateways and agreements
items.source: ICO Data sharing code of practice; Digital Economy Act 2017; UK GDPR Articles 5, 6 and 35
items.body:
Sharing personal data between organisations is lawful only if it meets data protection rules and the sharing body has legal power to do it. For a public authority, this means checking three things: that it has a legal gateway or power to share (a statute, a common law power or a statutory function), that the sharing meets the UK GDPR principles with a lawful basis, and that the sharing is necessary and proportionate for a stated purpose.

The ICO's Data Sharing Code of Practice recommends a data sharing agreement for regular sharing, setting out the purpose, what data is shared, who gets it, how it is kept secure, how long it is held and how people's rights are met. Such agreements are not a legal requirement, but they are good practice and help to show accountability. One-off requests may be handled with a documented decision instead.

A DPIA is normally needed for large-scale or high-risk sharing. It should be done before the sharing starts.

The Digital Economy Act 2017 gives specific powers to share data for public service delivery, debt, fraud and research, with codes of practice and safeguards. It does not remove the need to follow the UK GDPR.

Share the minimum necessary. If you can achieve the purpose with anonymised data, use it. Anonymised data, from which individuals cannot be identified, falls outside the UK GDPR. Pseudonymised data, where names are replaced by codes but a key can reverse this, is still personal data. Aggregation to counts can also protect identity, but small numbers can still reveal individuals.

Individuals must be told about sharing through privacy notices, unless an exemption applies. Check that the receiving organisation is a controller or processor, and what it may do with the data. Record each decision, including why it was lawful, so the department can explain it later.

Use secure transfer methods agreed in the agreement, and apply the classification marking.

That the request came in by post

questions.hint: Both a legal power and a UK GDPR lawful basis are needed.

questions.hint: These matters show the sharing is controlled and accountable.

options.text: It is special category data

questions.hint: If re-identification is possible, protections still apply.

questions.hint: The regulation applies to information relating to identifiable people.

questions.hint: Statistical disclosure control looks at small counts that can reveal individuals.

items.title: L8: Security clearances and baseline checks
items.source: HMG Baseline Personnel Security Standard (BPSS); UK Security Vetting guidance; Government Security Classifications Policy
items.body:
Security vetting tells a department that a person can be trusted with sensitive information or access. There are several levels. The Baseline Personnel Security Standard (BPSS) is not a security clearance but a set of pre-employment checks that all civil servants must pass. It checks identity, nationality and immigration status (the right to work), employment history for the past three years, and unspent criminal convictions. It is the minimum standard for access to OFFICIAL information.

The higher levels are formal national security vetting. Counter-Terrorist Check (CTC) is for those who work in sensitive posts or with regular access to certain sites. Security Check (SC) allows long-term access to SECRET assets and occasional access to TOP SECRET. Developed Vetting (DV) allows regular and frequent access to TOP SECRET and is based on much deeper enquiries, including interviews. Enhanced versions add checks such as finance.

Vetting is for a particular post, and a clearance is linked to the department that sponsors it. Clearances are reviewed and expire, and applicants should disclose any change in circumstances, such as a new partner or an overseas move.

A clearance is not a licence to see everything: access to classified material still depends on a need to know. Holding a higher clearance does not remove that requirement.

Vetting also considers factors such as honesty, financial pressures and susceptibility to pressure. Applicants must give full and accurate details. A failure to disclose information can be treated more seriously than the information itself. Vetting decisions are made on a risk basis, so a past problem does not automatically lead to refusal.

Information given for vetting is itself sensitive and is protected under data protection law.

options.text: Counter-Terrorist Check
The Baseline Personnel Security Standard

questions.hint: BPSS is the baseline standard and is not a formal clearance.

questions.hint: Clearance shows trust, not a right of access.

questions.hint: Clearance holders should disclose relevant changes so risks can be assessed.

items.title: L8: Briefing for Parliamentary questions and Q&A
items.source: Ministerial Code; Civil Service Code; House of Commons guidance on parliamentary questions
items.body:
Members of both Houses can put questions to ministers. Written questions are answered in writing, and oral questions are answered in the chamber. Officials draft answers and briefing for ministers, who are responsible to Parliament for what is said. A departmental answer should be accurate, relevant and complete, and in plain language.

For a written question, answer exactly what is asked, using the wording of the question. If the information is not held or can only be provided at disproportionate cost, say so. Check each figure against its source and clear the answer with the relevant policy and analytical teams. Define the terms and the time period, as 'in the last year' needs a start and end date. If a figure comes from a published statistic, cite the publication.

For an oral question, the minister will want a short 'line to take' with key points that answer the question, a few supporting facts, and a defensive line for follow-up questions. Prepare for the questions that might follow, called supplementaries. A Q&A section lists likely questions with proposed answers. Include any difficult facts, such as errors, rather than hiding them, so that the minister is not caught out. Give 'no surprises' warnings in advance.

The Ministerial Code requires ministers to be accurate and truthful with Parliament, and ministers who find they have inadvertently misled Parliament should correct the record at the earliest opportunity. The Civil Service Code requires officials to provide information and advice honestly and objectively. So if you spot an error in an answer already given, tell your senior officials at once so a correction can be considered.

Do not speculate or invent figures to fill a gap. If you do not know, say you will find out. Do not commit the minister to action without clearance. Keep the briefing within the classification rules, since a Q&A pack can include sensitive lines.

questions.hint: Accurate, focused answers meet the minister's duty to Parliament.

questions.hint: Errors should be corrected at the earliest opportunity.

questions.prompt: Why should a Q&A pack include difficult facts?

questions.hint: The Ministerial Code sets this duty, and officials support it.

questions.hint: Commitments need agreement from those responsible.
